lessons.title: Promise States: Pending, Fulfilled, Rejected
lessons.description: A Promise is a placeholder for a future value — it starts pending and settles as either fulfilled or rejected.

sections.heading: The three states
paragraphs: A Promise represents an async operation that hasn't completed yet. It starts in a pending state and can transition to one of two final states.
list: Pending — the operation is still in progress
Fulfilled — the operation completed successfully with a result value
Rejected — the operation failed with an error reason
Once settled, the state never changes again

codeExamples.heading: Promise states in action
explanation: The Promise constructor takes a function with resolve and reject callbacks.
The state change is irreversible — a fulfilled promise stays fulfilled.
codeExamples.output:
> resolve("Data loaded!")
> reject(new Error("Failed"))
fulfilled
rejected

practice.task: Create a Promise that resolves after 2 seconds with the message "Done!". Log the result using .then().
hints: The message should appear after 2 seconds.

keyTakeaways: Promises have three states: pending, fulfilled, and rejected.
A Promise settles once and never changes state again.
Use .then() for success and .catch() for errors.
Promises are the foundation of modern async JavaScript.
lessons.challenge: Create a Promise that randomly resolves or rejects after 1 second. Handle both outcomes with .then() and .catch().

lessons.title: Creating Promises with the new Promise Constructor
lessons.description: Wrap any async operation in a Promise to gain control over its resolution and rejection.

sections.heading: The Promise constructor
paragraphs: You create a Promise with new Promise(executor). The executor function receives two callbacks: resolve to signal success and reject to signal failure.
list: The executor runs immediately when the Promise is created
resolve(value) — fulfills the Promise with a value
reject(reason) — rejects the Promise with an Error
You can call only one — calling both does nothing on the second call
Errors thrown in the executor automatically reject the Promise

codeExamples.heading: Wrapping a callback in a Promise
explanation: The delay function wraps setTimeout in a Promise.
The fetchUser function wraps a callback pattern in a Promise.
Promises let you chain async operations cleanly.
Thrown errors in the executor automatically become rejections.

practice.task: Write a readFile(path) function that returns a Promise. Simulate success (80% chance) or failure (20% chance) with setTimeout.
hints: Use Math.random() to determine success or failure.
Resolve with file content or reject with an error.

keyTakeaways: Only the first resolve/reject call has effect.
Errors thrown in the executor automatically reject the Promise.
lessons.challenge: Write a retry function that tries an async operation up to N times before rejecting.

lessons.title: Promise Chaining: .then(), .catch(), and .finally()
lessons.description: Chain Promises together to create clean, readable async sequences.

sections.heading: How promise chaining works
paragraphs: .then() returns a new Promise, so you can chain multiple operations. Each .then() receives the resolved value from the previous one.
list: .then(fn) — runs when the Promise resolves, returns a new Promise
.catch(fn) — runs on any rejection in the chain
.finally(fn) — runs regardless of success or failure
Errors bubble down the chain until caught by a .catch()

codeExamples.heading: Promise chaining
explanation: Each .then() passes its result to the next one in the chain.
Return a Promise from .then() to chain async operations.
Errors bubble to the nearest .catch() in the chain.
.finally() runs whether the chain succeeded or failed.

practice.task: Chain 3 Promises: get a user, get their orders, then get order details. Use a single .catch() at the end for all errors.
hints: Each .then() should return the next Promise.
Pass the result to the next .then() via the return value.
One .catch() at the end handles errors from any step.

keyTakeaways: Each .then() returns a new Promise, enabling chaining.
Return a Promise from .then() to chain async operations.
Errors bubble down the chain until caught by .catch().
.finally() runs regardless of success or failure — great for cleanup.
lessons.challenge: Build a chained Promise that simulates: login → fetch profile → fetch dashboard data, with error handling at each step.

lessons.title: Promise Utilities: Promise.resolve(), Promise.reject(), Promise.withResolvers()
lessons.description: Utility methods for creating and managing Promises in common patterns.

sections.heading: Promise utility methods
list: These simplify common patterns and make code more readable

codeExamples.heading: Promise utilities
explanation: Promise.resolve() wraps a value in an already-resolved Promise.
Promise.withResolvers() gives you the resolve/reject functions externally.
withResolvers is great for wrapping event-based or callback-based APIs.

practice.task: Use Promise.withResolvers() to wrap a button click into a Promise. The Promise resolves when the button is clicked.

keyTakeaways: These are useful for converting values to Promises in chains.
Use withResolvers() to wrap callback or event-based APIs in Promises.
lessons.challenge: Use Promise.withResolvers() to wrap a setTimeout into a Promise and chain it with other async operations.
